title: Measures and units: length, area, volume, mass, time
goals: Change between mm, cm, m and km, g and kg, ml and litres, by multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1000
Change hours to minutes and back, remembering that time goes in 60s, not 100s
Put mixed units into one unit before adding or taking away
Work out the perimeter and area of a rectangle and the volume of a box, and turn cm³ into litres
Turn old inches, feet, miles and pints into metric
summary:
**Metric prefixes**: **kilo** (k) is a thousand, **centi** (c) a hundredth, **milli** (m) a thousandth.

- Length: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm, 1 cm = 10 mm. Drawings are in mm.
- Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 tonne = 1000 kg.
- Volume: 1 litre = 1000 ml.

**Converting**: multiply by a factor worth 1, like $\frac{1000\text{ mm}}{1\text{ m}}$. **Big unit to small** (m to mm): more of them, so **multiply**. **Small to big** (g to kg): fewer, so **divide**. 1.25 m = 1250 mm; 3200 g = 3.2 kg.

**Mixed units**: put everything in one unit before you add or take away. 1.5 m − 1440 mm: 1500 − 1440 = 60 mm.

**Time goes in 60s**: 1 min = 60 s, 1 h = 60 min, 1 day = 24 h. Hours to minutes: × 60. 2.5 h = 2 h 30 min, not 2 h 50 min; 0.75 h = 45 min.

**Perimeter** is the distance round a shape (a length). **Area** is the surface it covers, in squares (m², cm², mm²). For a rectangle, length $L$ and width $W$ in the same unit:

$$A = L \times W \qquad P = 2L + 2W$$

Area units: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = **10 000 cm²** = 1 000 000 mm². 1 cm² = 100 mm².

**Volume** is the space inside, in cubes. For a box: $V = L \times W \times H$.

- 1 litre = 1000 cm³ (a 10 cm cube); 1 ml = 1 cm³
- 1 m³ = 1000 litres
- 1 litre of water is about 1 kg

**Old units still about**: 1 inch = **25.4 mm** exactly; 1 foot = 12 inches = 304.8 mm; 1 mile ≈ 1.61 km; 1 UK pint ≈ 568 ml (a US pint is 473 ml); 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb. Feet and inches: all into inches first, then × 25.4.

**Sense check** every answer: mm numbers are big, m numbers small; a smaller unit always needs more of them.

formulas.name: Area of a rectangle
formulas.says: The area is the length times the width. It counts how many unit squares cover the shape.
symbols: the width, in the same unit as the length
formulas.example: a plate 3 m by 2 m: $A = 3 \times 2 = 6$ m².

formulas.name: Perimeter of a rectangle
formulas.says: The distance all the way round: two lengths and two widths added up.
symbols: the perimeter (a length: m, cm or mm)
the width, in the same unit
formulas.example: a guard panel 1.2 m by 0.8 m: $P = 2.4 + 1.6 = 4$ m of edge trim.

formulas.name: Volume of a box (cuboid)
formulas.says: The space inside a box shape is its length times its width times its height. It counts how many unit cubes fill it.
symbols: the volume (m³, cm³ or mm³; 1000 cm³ is a litre)
the height, all three in the same unit
formulas.example: a tank 50 cm by 40 cm by 30 cm: $V = 50 \times 40 \times 30 = 60\,000$ cm³, which is 60 litres.

bench.task: Measure a rectangular tub or parts tray on the bench, work out how many litres it holds, then check it with water from a measuring jug. Cold water only, on a bench with no electrics or machines nearby; mop up any spill.
check: Measure the inside length, width and depth with a steel rule, in mm
Work out $V = L \times W \times H$ in cm³, then ÷ 1000 for litres
Fill it with a measuring jug, counting the litres, and compare with your answer
Work out what the water weighs (about 1 kg a litre) before you try to lift it

bench.task: Measure a bench top or a sheet of board with a tape. Work out its perimeter in metres and its area in m².
check: Measure the length and width in mm
Sense check: a bench top is usually between 1 and 3 m²

cards.q: Have a go: a guess is fine. A steel plate is 1.25 m long. How long is it in millimetres (mm)?
cards.why: There are 1000 mm in a metre, so multiply by 1000: $1.25 \times 1000 = 1250$ mm. 125 is × 100, which gives centimetres (125 cm), not mm. 12.5 and 12 500 move the decimal point the wrong number of places.

cards.title: Metric units and their prefixes
cards.body:
Metric units are built from a few base units. A **prefix** in front says how many.

- **kilo** (k) means a thousand: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 kg = 1000 g.
- **centi** (c) means a hundredth: 100 cm = 1 m.
- **milli** (m) means a thousandth: 1000 mm = 1 m, 1000 ml = 1 litre.

The base units:

- **length** in metres (m)
- **mass** (how heavy) in grams (g) and kilograms (kg); a **tonne** (t) is 1000 kg
- **volume** (how much a container holds) in litres (L)

On engineering drawings lengths are in **mm**. And 1 cm = 10 mm.
cards.more:
Think of money. A penny is a hundredth of a pound, just as a centimetre is a hundredth of a metre. So 100 pence make £1, and 100 cm make 1 m.

Milli goes one step further: a thousandth. A metre rule has 1000 little mm marks on it, 10 in every cm.

Worked numbers:

- a 2.4 m length of box section is 240 cm, or 2400 mm
- a 25 kg bag of cement is 25 000 g
- a 1 tonne lifting sling is rated for 1000 kg
- a 5 litre can of cutting oil holds 5000 ml

The same three prefixes turn up everywhere: kilo-watts, milli-amps, milli-seconds. Learn them once.

cards.q: Match each amount to the same amount in a smaller unit.
cards.why: Kilo is a thousand, centi a hundredth, milli a thousandth. The one that trips people is 1 cm = 10 mm: a centimetre is only ten millimetres, not a hundred.

cards.title: Changing units: multiply or divide
cards.body:
To change units, multiply by a **conversion factor**: a fraction worth exactly 1, such as $\frac{1000\text{ mm}}{1\text{ m}}$. The amount stays the same; only the unit changes.

The quick rule:

- **Big unit to small unit** (m to mm): you need **more** of them, so **multiply**. 2.5 m = $2.5 \times 1000$ = 2500 mm.
- **Small unit to big unit** (g to kg): you need **fewer**, so **divide**. 3200 g = $3200 \div 1000$ = 3.2 kg.

× 1000 moves the decimal point 3 places right; ÷ 1000 moves it 3 places left. For 100, two places; for 10, one.

**Mixed units**: before you add or take away, put both amounts in the **same unit**.
cards.more:
Why a fraction worth 1? 1000 mm and 1 m are the same length, so $\frac{1000\text{ mm}}{1\text{ m}}$ is 1. Multiplying by 1 never changes an amount.

Pick the fraction that has the unit you are getting rid of on the **bottom**, so it cancels:

$$3200\text{ g} \times \frac{1\text{ kg}}{1000\text{ g}} = \frac{3200}{1000}\text{ kg} = 3.2\text{ kg}$$

The g on top and the g on the bottom cancel, and kg is left.

Sense check: a kilogram is big, so there should be fewer of them. 3.2 is fewer than 3200. Right.

Mixed units: a 1.6 m bar with 85 cm cut off. 85 cm is 0.85 m, and $1.60 - 0.85 = 0.75$ m left. Taking 85 from 1.6 would be nonsense.

cards.q: A box of fixings is marked {g} g. What does it weigh in kg?
cards.why: Grams to kilograms is small unit to big unit: fewer of them, so **divide** by 1000. Multiplying gives {wrong}, which is far more kilograms than a box of fixings could weigh.

cards.title: Time goes in 60s, not 100s
cards.body:
1 minute = 60 seconds, 1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 day = 24 hours, 1 week = 7 days.

So a decimal of an hour is **not** a number of minutes:

- 0.5 h is half of 60: 30 min
- 0.25 h = 15 min, and 0.75 h = 45 min
- 2.5 h is 2 h 30 min, **not** 2 h 50 min

Hours to minutes: **× 60**. Minutes to hours: **÷ 60**.

Adding times: add the minutes, then turn every 60 minutes into an hour. Jobs of 45, 10, 8, 65, 20 and 35 min make 183 min. That is 3 lots of 60 (180) with 3 left over: **3 h 3 min**.
cards.more:
Picture a clock face. Half way round is 30 minutes, not 50. A quarter of the way round is 15 minutes. That is why 2.5 hours is two and a half hours: 2 h 30 min.

Worked number: a test rig runs for 1.75 h. $1.75 \times 60 = 105$ min, which is 1 h 45 min.

Big jumps work the same way, one step at a time. How many minutes in 9 weeks?

$$9 \times 7 \times 24 \times 60 = 90\,720\text{ min}$$

weeks to days (× 7), days to hours (× 24), hours to minutes (× 60).

A pump that runs day and night for 2 weeks clocks up $2 \times 7 \times 24 = 336$ hours: useful for service intervals.

cards.q: A soak test runs for {h} hours. How many minutes is that?
cards.why: Hours to minutes: × 60. {h} h is {answer} min. Treating the hour as 100 minutes gives {wrong}, the most common slip with time.

cards.title: Perimeter and area of a rectangle
cards.body:
**Perimeter** is the distance **round** a shape: the length of edge trim or fencing. It is a length, in m or mm.

**Area** is the **surface** a shape covers: the sheet steel, the paint, the floor. It is counted in **squares**. A square metre (m²) is a square 1 m each way.

A plate 3 m by 2 m holds 3 rows of 2 one-metre squares: 6 m².

For a **rectangle** (four square corners), length $L$ and width $W$:

$$A = L \times W \qquad P = 2L + 2W$$

The perimeter is two lengths plus two widths. Put $L$ and $W$ in the same unit first.
cards.more:
Picture an ant walking round the edge of a 1 cm square tile. It walks 4 cm: that is the perimeter. The tile covers 1 cm²: that is the area. Different questions, different units.

Worked number: a guard panel 1.2 m by 0.8 m.

- Area: $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$ m² of mesh
- Perimeter: $2 \times 1.2 + 2 \times 0.8 = 2.4 + 1.6 = 4$ m of edge trim

Careful with area units. A square metre is 100 cm each way, so it holds 100 rows of 100 cm² squares:

$$1\text{ m}^2 = 100 \times 100 = 10\,000\text{ cm}^2$$

not 100. In mm, $1000 \times 1000 = 1\,000\,000$ mm². And 1 cm² = 100 mm².

cards.q: A workshop bay floor is {L} m long and {W} m wide. It is to be painted. What is its area?
cards.why: Paint covers a surface, so you want the **area**: length times width, {answer} m². Two lengths plus two widths ({per} m) is the perimeter: the distance round the edge, which is what you would need for a painted border line, not the floor.

cards.title: Volume and litres
cards.body:
**Volume** is the space inside: how much a tank or a box holds. It is counted in **cubes**. A cube 1 cm each way is 1 cubic centimetre (cm³).

For a box shape (a **cuboid**):

$$V = L \times W \times H$$

length times width times height, all in the same unit.

Liquids use **litres**. A litre fills a cube 10 cm each way: $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ cm³. So:

- 1 litre = 1000 cm³, and 1 ml = 1 cm³
- 1 m³ = 1000 litres
- 1 litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg
cards.more:
Picture a cube 3 cm each way, cut into 1 cm cubes. There are 3 layers, each 3 by 3: $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ little cubes. So its volume is 27 cm³. Length times width times height counts the cubes for you.

Worked number: a coolant tank is 50 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm deep inside.

$$V = 50 \times 40 \times 30 = 60\,000\text{ cm}^3$$

A litre is 1000 cm³, so $60\,000 \div 1000 = 60$ litres. Full of water it holds about 60 kg: too heavy for one person to lift.

Why is 1 m³ a thousand litres? A metre is ten 10 cm lengths, so a cubic metre holds $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ litre cubes.

cards.q: A coolant tank measures {L} cm long, {W} cm wide and {H} cm deep inside. How many litres does it hold when full?
cards.hint: Work out the volume in cm³ first. How many cm³ make a litre?
cards.why: Length × width × height gives {cc} cm³. A litre is 1000 cm³, so divide by 1000: {answer} litres. Leaving it at {cc} would be the answer in cm³ (or ml), not litres.

cards.title: Old units you still meet
cards.body:
The UK went metric, but older **imperial** units are still about:

- **Inches** and **feet** on old drawings, imperial bolts and tools: 1 inch (in or ") = **25.4 mm** exactly; 1 foot (ft) = 12 inches = 304.8 mm.
- **Miles** on road signs: 1 mile ≈ 1.61 km.
- **Pints** of milk: 1 UK pint ≈ 568 ml. An American pint is smaller: 473 ml.
- **Pounds** (lb): 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.

They work the same way: multiply by the factor. 3 inches is $3 \times 25.4 = 76.2$ mm.

For feet and inches, turn it all into inches first: 2 ft 6 in is 30 in, and $30 \times 25.4 = 762$ mm.
cards.more:
An inch is about the width of a thumb, roughly 2.5 cm. That is a good sense check: the mm answer is always about 25 times the inches.

The fraction method works here too. 4 inches to mm:

$$4\text{ in} \times \frac{25.4\text{ mm}}{1\text{ in}} = 101.6\text{ mm}$$

Going back, divide: 50 mm is $50 \div 25.4 \approx 1.97$ inches, just under 2.

Feet and inches are mixed units, like hours and minutes. 5 ft 4 in is $5 \times 12 + 4 = 64$ inches, not 54: a foot is 12 inches, not 10.

Miles: a site 20 miles away is about $20 \times 1.61 \approx 32$ km.

cards.q: An old drawing gives a hole spacing of {i} inches. What is that in mm?
cards.why: One inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so multiply: {answer} mm. Sense check: about 25 times the number of inches. Using 2.54 gives the answer in cm, ten times too small for mm.

cards.q: You need 6 brackets cut from flat bar, each 240 mm long. You have a 1.5 m length of bar. Ignoring the saw cuts, how much is left over?

steps.ask: Put everything in one unit: mm, the unit on the drawing.
Work out how much you cut.
Give it in metres, if asked.

steps.show: 1440 mm is just under 1.5 m, so a short offcut of 60 mm makes sense.

cards.why: One unit first, then the sums, then change back if the question wants another unit. Trying $1.5 - 1440$ mixes metres and millimetres and gives nonsense.

cards.context: From the worked example: 6 brackets of 240 mm (1440 mm in all) from a 1.5 m bar. Step 1 turned the 1.5 m into 1500 mm.
cards.q: Why must the 1.5 m be turned into 1500 mm before you take away 1440 mm? Say it in your own words.
cards.model: You can only take away amounts in the same unit, just as you cannot take pounds from pence without changing one of them. 1.5 m and 1440 mm are both lengths, but the numbers count different-sized steps. Put into mm, the bar is 1500 mm, and 1500 − 1440 = 60 mm is left. Taking 1440 from 1.5 would give a negative length, which cannot be right: the bar plainly holds all six brackets.
points: You can only add or take away amounts in the same unit
1.5 m is 1500 mm (big unit to small: × 1000)
Doing it without converting gives a result that fails a sense check

cards.q: 8 spacers, each 175 mm long, are cut from a 2 m bar. Ignoring the saw cuts, how much is left, in m?

steps.ask: Work out how much you cut.

cards.why: Same method: one unit, the sums, then back to metres. 600 mm is 0.6 m (÷ 1000: small unit to big unit).

cards.q: You cut {n} pieces, each {p} mm long, from a {L} m bar. Ignoring the saw cuts, how many mm are left?
cards.hint: Turn the bar into mm first.
cards.work: Bar: ${{L}} \times 1000 = {{lmm}}$ mm. Cut: ${{n}} \times {{p}} = {{cut}}$ mm. Left: ${{lmm}} - {{cut}} = {{answer}}$ mm
cards.why: Everything into mm first: the bar is {lmm} mm. The pieces use {cut} mm, leaving {answer} mm. Forgetting to convert the {L} m makes the subtraction meaningless.

cards.q: A mesh guard panel is {L} m long and {W} cm high. What length of edge trim goes all the way round it, in metres?
cards.hint: Put the height into metres first. How many cm in a metre?
cards.why: All the way round is the **perimeter**: two lengths and two widths. First make the units match: {W} cm is {wm} m (÷ 100). Adding {L} and {W} as they stand mixes metres and centimetres; multiplying them gives an area, not a length.

cards.q: A cover plate is {L} mm by {W} mm. What is its area in cm²?
cards.hint: Turn each side into cm before you multiply. 10 mm make 1 cm.
cards.work: {L} mm = {lc} cm and {W} mm = {wc} cm. $A = {{lc}} \times {{wc}} = {{answer}}$ cm²
cards.why: Change the lengths first (÷ 10 each), then multiply: {answer} cm². Or work in mm² ({mm2} mm²) and divide by **100**, because 1 cm² is 10 mm by 10 mm. Dividing the mm² by 10 is the usual slip: it treats area units like lengths.

cards.q: Someone added up two job times for a timesheet. One line has a mistake in it. Which?
lines: Job A took 1 h 45 min; job B took 2 h 30 min.
75 min is 0.75 h, so the total is 3.75 h
cards.fix: 75 min is 1 h 15 min, so the total is 4 h 15 min (4.25 h)
cards.why: Minutes are not hundredths of an hour. 75 min is more than an hour: 60 min make 1 h, with 15 min over, and 15 min is 0.25 h. The check: any number of minutes over 60 must add at least one whole hour, so the total must be more than 4 h.

cards.q: Why is 1 m² equal to 10 000 cm², and not 100 cm²?
options: Area units always go up in steps of ten
A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm
Only 100 cm² fit along one edge
A square has four sides of 25 cm
cards.why: A square metre is 100 cm long **and** 100 cm wide, so it holds 100 rows of 100 one-centimetre squares: $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm². Converting 100 is right for a length, but an area has two lengths multiplied, so the factor is used twice. The same goes for mm: 1 cm² = $10 \times 10 = 100$ mm².

cards.q: Which measure does each job need?
pairs: the edge trim round a guard panel
the paint to cover a floor
how heavy a box of bolts is
cards.why: Round the edge is a length; covering a surface is an area, in squares; filling a space is a volume, in cubes or litres; how heavy is a mass. Mixing up perimeter and area is the common slip.

cards.q: A machine ran for {h} h {m} min on one job. How many minutes is that in all?
cards.why: Hours to minutes is × 60, then add the minutes left over: {answer} min. Writing it as {wrong} treats an hour as 100 minutes. This is a mixed unit, like feet and inches: turn the big unit into the small one, then add.

cards.q: A water tank measures {L} m by {W} m by {H} m inside. Full of water, about what mass of water does it hold, in kg?
cards.hint: Volume in m³, then litres (1 m³ is 1000 litres), then about 1 kg for each litre.
cards.why: Three steps: volume in m³ ({m3}), × 1000 for litres, and each litre of water is about 1 kg: {answer} kg. Stopping at {m3} is the volume in m³, not a mass. Worth knowing before anyone tries to move a full tank.

cards.q: An old drawing of a machine base gives a length of {ft} ft {i} in. What is that in mm?
cards.hint: Turn it all into inches first. How many inches in a foot?
cards.why: Feet and inches are mixed units: {ft} ft is {ft} × 12 inches, plus {i}, makes {tot} inches. Then × 25.4 for mm: {answer} mm. Treating a foot as 10 inches is the slip, the same one as treating an hour as 100 minutes.

cards.q: A cut list says {mm} mm. What is that in metres?
cards.why: Small unit to big unit: fewer of them, so divide by 1000 (the decimal point moves 3 places left). {mm} mm is {answer} m.

cards.q: A steel sheet is {L} m long and {W} cm wide. What is its area in m²?
cards.why: Same units first: {W} cm is {wm} m. Then length × width: {answer} m². Multiplying {L} by {W} as they stand mixes units and gives a number 100 times too big.

cards.q: A job took 1.75 hours. How long is that in hours and minutes?
cards.why: 0.75 of an hour is $0.75 \times 60 = 45$ min, so 1 h 45 min. 1 h 75 min reads the decimal as minutes, and 2 h 15 min is what you get if you then turn those 75 minutes into an hour and a quarter.
